page.title: Healthchecks: a cron job monitor, mapped

slots.overviewDescription: Healthchecks in context: the jobs that ping it, the people it alerts and what it is made of.
slots.mapDescription: The Django web app, the background loops and the database, with the paths a ping, a missed ping and an alert take.
slots.completionLessons:
• Why a silent job is noticed by a loop, not by a request
  • How one row update turns into an alert
  • Why the alert loop can run twice without sending twice
slots.completionIntro: You followed a ping into the database, watched a job go quiet and traced the alert out to a person.

panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

Pings in, alerts out

One Django project runs as four processes from the same code: the web server and three management commands. They share nothing but the database.

How to read it

Jobs and people on the left, the web app and the background loops in the middle, the database and outside services on the right. A ping only writes a row; deciding that a job is late is the alert loop's job.

people.title: Jobs and people
people.text: Two kinds of user: the scheduled jobs that report in, and the team that sets up checks and wants to hear when one goes quiet.

intake.title: Take a ping
intake.line1: An HTTP request or an email
intake.text: Two doors for the same event: an HTTP request to the check's URL, or an email to its address. Both end in the same call.

web.title: Web app
web.text: The part people see: the live dashboard, the REST API, logins and teams, and the pages that connect Slack, email or a webhook.

watch.title: Decide who is late
watch.text: The check's rules turn its last ping and schedule into a deadline; a loop that never sleeps longer than two seconds finds the checks past theirs.

notify.title: Tell someone
notify.text: One transport per integration sends the alert; a second loop mails monthly, weekly or daily reports and reminders while something stays down.

storage.title: Storage
storage.text: Every process reads and writes the same database; large ping bodies can go to S3-compatible storage instead.

nodes.what: Anything that runs on a schedule and can make one HTTP request or send one email when it finishes: curl -fsS https://hc-ping.com/<uuid> at the end of a crontab line.
nodes.why: Healthchecks never calls the job. It only listens, so it works behind any firewall, and silence is the signal.
nodes.tools: curl · wget · an email client · /start, /fail, /<exit code>

nodes.what: Creates checks with a period and a grace time (or a cron expression), connects channels, and gets the alert when a job goes quiet.
nodes.why: The whole point of the service is to reach this person when nobody else would notice a job that stopped running.
nodes.tools: Browser · phone · the REST API with a project API key

nodes.what: /ping/<uuid> and its variants. Works out what the request means (success, start, fail, log or ignore) from the path, the exit code, the method (a POST-only check ignores other methods) and, when the check filters on it, keywords in the body, then hands it to the check. An unknown UUID gets a 404.
nodes.why: It must answer fast and be easy to call from any job: no login (the UUID is the secret), no CSRF, any method, CORS open. All the logic lives one call further.

nodes.what: A small SMTP server. An email to <uuid>@your-host is a ping; subject or body keywords can turn it into a start or a failure.
nodes.why: Some jobs (backup appliances, NAS boxes) can only send email. They get the same check as a curl call.

nodes.what: One row per monitored job: its period, grace and schedule, its last ping and its status. Check.ping() records a ping; get_status() and going_down_after() turn the last ping into a deadline.
nodes.why: Every process imports the same model, so the web app and the alert loop agree on what late means.

nodes.what: My Checks, check details and the event log. The page asks for every check's status every 3 seconds for a short while after the tab becomes visible or the user is active, every 60 seconds otherwise, and redraws only what changed.
nodes.why: Status is computed on read from the last ping, so the dashboard can show a check as late a moment before the alert loop has noticed.

nodes.what: Create, update, pause and list checks, read pings and flips. A request carries a project API key in X-Api-Key (or api_key in the JSON body); read-only keys see but cannot change. Status badges and a Prometheus metrics URL are read with a key in the URL, without logging in.
nodes.why: Teams create checks from their deploy scripts, so a new cron job gets monitored without anyone opening the dashboard.

nodes.what: Sign-up by email link, passwords, WebAuthn and TOTP, projects with members and read-only access, API keys, report settings.
nodes.why: A check belongs to a project, not a person, so a team keeps its checks when someone leaves.

nodes.what: One folder per integration with its own pages: connect Slack by OAuth, verify an email address, type a webhook URL. Each saves a Channel row with its settings in a text field, JSON for most kinds. Telegram also takes calls in: its bot posts to /integrations/telegram/bot/ to link a chat.
nodes.why: Adding an integration means adding a folder, not touching the alert loop.

nodes.what: A loop that never stops: find checks whose deadline has passed and mark them down (a flip), then claim each unprocessed flip and hand it to a pool of worker threads.
nodes.why: A job that stops running sends nothing, so no request ever arrives to react to. Something has to look at the clock.

nodes.what: Channel.notify() records a Notification, calls the channel's transport (Slack, email, Telegram, webhook and about 25 more) and saves the error, if any, on the channel.
nodes.why: Each transport only knows how to format and post one message; retries, timing and bookkeeping are shared.

nodes.what: Monthly, weekly or daily summaries by email, and hourly or daily reminders while any check stays down.
nodes.why: An alert can be missed. A reminder that keeps coming until the job is fixed is the safety net.

nodes.what: Slack, Telegram, Discord, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, ntfy, Signal, SMS and phone calls, plain webhooks and more.
nodes.why: Teams already watch one of these; the alert has to land where they look.
nodes.tools: Mostly HTTPS APIs and webhooks; Signal through a local signal-cli socket

nodes.what: The SMTP relay that delivers email alerts, sign-in links, reports and nags. Bounces come back to POST /api/v1/bounces/, which marks the notification failed and, for a permanent failure, can switch the email channel or the reports off.
nodes.why: Email is the one channel every account has, so it carries the reports and the sign-in links too.

nodes.what: Checks, pings, flips, channels, notifications, users and projects. The only thing the four processes share. SQLite by default; PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB when DB is set.
nodes.why: Row locks and conditional updates in this database are what keep two processes from recording the same ping or sending the same alert twice.
nodes.tools: Django ORM · migrations in each app

nodes.what: Optional. With S3_BUCKET set, a ping body over 100 bytes is stored here under <check uuid>/ plus a sortable form of the ping number, and the database keeps only its size.
nodes.why: Not stated in the code, but probably: logs pasted into pings would otherwise swell the database.

checkin.title: A job checks in
checkin.desc: A cron job finishes and makes one request. The check's row moves its deadline forward and a ping row is added.

hops.t: The last command in the crontab line is curl -fsS https://hc-ping.com/<uuid>. The UUID is the only secret: whoever knows it can ping the check.

The view finds the check by UUID, reads the client address, method and body, and decides the action: success here. An exit code above 0, /fail or (when the check filters the body) a failure keyword would make it a failure.

Inside one transaction the check's row is locked, last_ping is set, the new deadline alert_after is computed from the period or the cron schedule plus grace, and a Ping row is written. The view answers OK.

fail.title: A job reports a failure
fail.desc: The job runs but fails and says so. The ping itself flips the check to down; the alert loop picks the flip up within seconds.

hops.t: The job ends with curl https://hc-ping.com/<uuid>/$?: the shell's exit code is part of the URL. Here it is 1.
A non-zero exit code makes the action fail. If the check filters the body, a failure keyword could have done the same.
The status was up and is now down, so create_flip() writes a Flip row (up to down, reason: fail) in the same transaction as the ping. Nothing is sent yet.
Within about two seconds, if a worker is free, the alert loop asks for a flip with no processed time, and claims it with a conditional update so a second sendalerts process cannot take it too.
The flip goes to one of the worker threads. The channels to notify are this check's channels that are enabled, fastest first, minus those that ignore this kind of change.
Before anything is sent, a Notification row records the attempt with its error set to Sending; the result replaces it afterwards.
The Slack transport posts a message with the check's name, its new status and the reason, its schedule, its total pings and its last ping with the body.
Someone on the team reads it in the channel they already watch.

quiet.title: A job goes quiet
quiet.desc: A job stops running and sends nothing. Nothing reaches the web app; the alert loop notices the deadline has passed.

hops.t: Every pass of the loop asks for the check with the earliest alert_after in the past that is not down yet. A partial index on alert_after keeps that query cheap.

The deadline is only a hint: get_status() recomputes the status from the last ping, the schedule and the grace time. If the check is only in grace, the loop moves alert_after to the real deadline and goes on.

It is down. One conditional update sets status = down only if the status is still what was read; if another process got there first, zero rows change and this one stops. Otherwise it writes the flip (reason: timeout).
On the next pass the loop claims that flip and gives it to a worker thread. By default there is one (--num-workers), so a slow send makes the next flip wait.
This check has an email channel with a verified address: the email transport sends the alert through the outgoing mail server.
And a Slack channel: the same flip goes out there too. A channel that answers with a permanent error is switched off.
The team hears about a job that failed silently, about one grace period after it should have run.

report.title: The periodic report
report.desc: A separate loop mails each account a summary of its checks, and reminders while something stays down.

hops.t: The loop looks for a profile whose next_report_date has passed, and moves that date forward with a conditional update: the process that wins the update sends the report.

The report lists every check in every project of the account with its downtime in each of the last two completed periods (months, weeks or days), not the current one. It is skipped when no check has been pinged for six months.

buildSteps.title: A ping counter
buildSteps.text: A table of checks, a URL per check, and a view that records the time of each request.
buildSteps.decision: The job calls the service, never the other way round: no agent, no open port on the job's side.

buildSteps.title: Someone to look at it
buildSteps.text: Accounts, projects and a dashboard that computes each check's status from its last ping.
buildSteps.decision: Status is derived on read, so the dashboard is right even when no background process runs.

buildSteps.title: Notice silence
buildSteps.text: A loop that finds checks past their deadline and records the change as a flip.
buildSteps.decision: A separate process with a while loop and the database as its queue: no Celery, no Redis.

buildSteps.title: Tell someone
buildSteps.text: Channels, a transport per integration and a pool of threads that send the alerts.
buildSteps.decision: One transport class per integration, so a slow webhook only holds up one worker thread.

buildSteps.title: More ways in
buildSteps.text: Pings by email, a REST API for scripts and an optional bucket for large ping bodies.
buildSteps.decision: Every door ends in the same Check.ping(), so the rules are written once.

buildSteps.title: Keep reminding
buildSteps.text: Periodic reports and repeating nags by email.
buildSteps.decision: Reports reuse the alert loop's trick: a conditional update decides which process sends.

tour.title: A monitor that waits for silence
body: Healthchecks watches scheduled jobs from the outside. Each job pings a URL when it runs; when a ping does not arrive on time, the team gets an alert.
Jobs and people on one side, notification services on the other, and in between a Django app, three background loops and one database.
tour.why: Most monitoring asks a service whether it is up. Here the job reports in, so a check works behind any firewall and the alert means: this did not happen.

tour.title: A ping writes two rows
body: Follow one successful run of a cron job into the database.
tour.why: The ping endpoint does almost nothing on purpose. It must answer in milliseconds and never make a job fail.

tour.title: A failure flips the check at once
body: The job says it failed, so the check goes down in the same transaction as the ping.
tour.why: A failure that is reported is the easy case: the request that carries the news also records the flip.

tour.title: Nobody calls: the loop looks at the clock
body: A job that stops running sends no request. The alert loop finds checks whose deadline has passed.
tour.why: This is why Healthchecks has a background process at all. The conditional update makes two copies of the loop safe.

tour.title: One flip, every channel
body: The flip is claimed once and sent to each of the check's channels from a worker thread.
tour.why: Alerts go out in parallel, fastest channels first, so one slow webhook does not delay the Slack message.

tour.title: Reports and nags
body: A second loop mails monthly, weekly or daily summaries and keeps reminding while something is down.
tour.why: An alert at 3 a.m. is easy to miss. A reminder every hour is not.

body: One Django codebase run as a web server and three loops, sharing a database.
The design choice that shapes everything: silence is detected by a loop, never by a request.

check.title: Inside the check: recording a ping
check.sub: What Check.ping() does with one ping, in order. The HTTP view and the email listener both end here.
check.cap: The check's row and the ping row are written in one transaction with the row locked, so the alert loop never sees a new last_ping without its ping, and two pings at once cannot deadlock.

steps.d: A transaction and select_for_update(); concurrent pings to one check wait in line.

steps.t: Paused and waiting for a manual resume?

steps.d: Remember when the run started and its run ID, to measure its duration later.
Set last_ping, compute the duration if the run ID matches the start.
Any change, new to up included, writes a Flip; the alert loop sends the ones that matter.
alert_after is the grace start plus grace: what the alert loop will look for.
Address, method, user agent, exit code; the body inline, or only its size when it goes to S3.
Outside the transaction, so a slow bucket does not hold the lock.
Pings beyond the plan's limit are deleted with their S3 bodies, and older notifications and flips with them.

sendalerts.title: Inside the alert loop
sendalerts.sub: One pass of sendalerts: first mark late checks down, then send the flips. It sleeps two seconds only when there is nothing to do.
sendalerts.cap: Both halves claim their work with a conditional UPDATE and check that exactly one row changed. That is the only coordination between several sendalerts processes, and it is enough.

steps.d: alert_after in the past, status not down, earliest first.
A crash here pushes alert_after an hour ahead and re-raises, which ends the command; once restarted, it skips that check for an hour.

exit.t: Move alert_after to the real deadline

steps.d: UPDATE … WHERE status is still the old one.
Dated when the check actually went down, not when the loop noticed.
Only if a worker seat is free; set processed where it is still empty.
Pick the channels and call each one's notify().

db.title: Inside the database: the alerting tables
db.sub: Five of the tables in hc/api/models.py. Hover a reference to see the table it points to.
db.cap: alert_after and processed each have a partial index (on rows that are not down, and on flips not yet processed), so the alert loop's two questions stay fast however many checks and flips there are.

fields.note: the secret in the ping URL
cron expression and its time zone
when the alert loop should look
null for success; start, fail, ign, log
or object_size when the body is in S3

tables.name: api_flip
tables.note: A status change, usually waiting to be sent.

fields.note: empty until sendalerts claims it; set at once for a pause
the integration's settings, JSON for most kinds

tables.name: api_notification
tables.note: One alert sent on one channel.

entries.t: Django's command line: runs the web server in development, the three background loops and one-off admin commands.
Almost every setting comes from an environment variable: database, email, S3, each integration's keys. An optional hc/local_settings.py can override them.
entries.why: One image serves every deployment; nothing is edited in the code.

entries.t: Mounts each app's URLs, one line per integration.
The core: the check, ping, flip and channel models, the ping endpoint and the REST API.
Check, Ping, Flip, Channel and Notification, with the status and deadline logic.
entries.why: Every process imports this file; reading Check.get_status() explains when anything alerts.

entries.t: The ping views and the REST API views, plus badges, bounces, metrics and status.
/ping/… and /api/v1…v3/.
Checks the X-Api-Key header and picks the API version.
The base classes every integration's transport builds on: HTTP with retries, templates, errors.

The background processes, each a Django management command, plus maintenance commands. Some of those (in hc/api/ and hc/accounts/) are meant to run from cron outside the container: pruning old data, flapping and inactivity notices.

entries.why: Without it nothing ever goes down by timeout; the dashboard would show it, but nobody would be told.
